opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to recognize is that uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. It's actually a reason for caution. When you look at the scientific community right now, you have very serious, competent researchers who disagree enormously about how likely catastrophic outcomes are, and about the timelines. Some think we're decades away from human-level capabilities; others think it could be just a few years. Some think loss of control is very unlikely; others think it's quite plausible. That disagreement itself is information. It tells us we don't understand what we're building well enough to rule out the bad scenarios.

And when the potential downside includes outcomes that are irreversible, things like large-scale misuse, or humanity losing control over systems that are smarter than us, then the rational response is the precautionary principle. We apply this reasoning in lots of other domains. If you're building a new bridge or approving a new drug, you don't say, "Well, we're not sure it will collapse, so let's go ahead." The burden of proof is on the developer to show that it's safe. With AI, we currently have it almost backwards: the companies race ahead, and the people raising concerns are expected to prove that harm will happen before anything is done.

So concretely, I think uncertainty should push us toward a few things. First, investing much more in the science of understanding and evaluating these systems, so that we can reduce the uncertainty, because right now we're largely flying blind. Second, putting in place governance mechanisms now, before we know for sure, things like transparency requirements, independent evaluations of dangerous capabilities, liability, and the ability for governments to intervene if certain thresholds are crossed. You don't want to be building the fire department after the fire has started. And third, I think we need to think seriously about designing AI systems that are safe by construction, for example systems that help us understand the world and answer questions without having their own goals and agency, rather than racing to build autonomous agents whose behavior we can't guarantee.

There's also a personal dimension to this for me. For a long time I didn't take these risks seriously, and then, after seeing how quickly capabilities advanced, I had to confront the possibility that I'd been wrong. And I thought about my children, my grandchild, and I asked myself: even if the probability is, say, ten percent, or even one percent, is that an acceptable risk to impose on everyone without their consent? I don't think it is. When the stakes are that high, even a modest probability should be enough to motivate serious action.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty is a reason for caution and that even a modest chance of catastrophic harm warrants serious action, then supports precautionary steps such as research, governance, and safer system design.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. It's actually the opposite. When I talk to people who are skeptical about catastrophic risks, they often say, "We don't know if this is going to happen, so why worry?" But that's not how we reason about risk in any other domain. If you're building a bridge, or a nuclear plant, or a new drug, you don't wait for proof that it will fail before you take precautions. You take precautions precisely because you can't be sure it's safe.

And I would say that the uncertainty here is genuine. I don't know whether we'll have AI systems that are dangerous in the ways people worry about in five years, or twenty years, or whether it will happen at all. Honest people disagree. Some of my colleagues, people I respect a lot, think the probability is very small. Others think it's quite high. I've come to believe that I can't rule it out, and that was actually a shift for me. For most of my career I didn't think very much about these questions. I was focused on making the methods work. And then around early 2023, when I saw how quickly the capabilities were advancing, I started to really look at the arguments, and I couldn't find a good reason to be confident that things would go well.

So how should that shape what we do? I think the key principle is that when the stakes are extremely high and potentially irreversible, you have to weight the bad outcomes much more heavily than their probability alone would suggest. If there's even a 10 percent chance, or a 5 percent chance, or honestly even a 1 percent chance of something catastrophic for humanity, that's not acceptable. We would never accept that for an airplane. And here we're talking about something that could affect everyone, that we might not get a second chance to correct.

The other point is about how to act under that uncertainty, because there's a trap where people say, "If we don't know, let's just wait and see." But the problem is that the information we need may arrive too late. By the time it's obvious that a system is dangerous, it may already be deployed everywhere, or we may already have lost the ability to control it. So I think we need to invest very seriously, right now, in the science of understanding these systems. That's partly why I've been pushing for things like the international scientific report on AI safety, so we can have a shared, honest picture of what we know and what we don't.

And then I think precaution means a few concrete things. It means governments should require evidence of safety before the most powerful systems are deployed, not after. It means we need to be very careful about systems that are agentic, that have goals and act in the world, because that's where a lot of the hardest-to-control risks come from. And it means we should be developing alternative approaches. I've been working on what I call Scientist AI, which is the idea of building systems that are more like a very good scientist than an agent — systems that try to understand the world and give us trustworthy answers, but that don't have their own objectives they're pursuing. I think that's a way to get a lot of the benefits while reducing the risks.

But the honest answer is that we're flying somewhat blind, and we're moving very fast, and that combination is what worries me. Uncertainty should make us humble, and humility, in this case, means slowing down enough to understand what we're building.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that uncertainty is a reason to take precautions, emphasizing the catastrophic stakes and calling for safety evidence and serious investment in understanding AI systems.

astra-6.text:
I think uncertainty is a reason to be cautious, rather than a reason to do nothing. We don’t need to know with certainty that a system will cause a catastrophe before taking precautions. What matters is both how likely the harm is and how large it could be. If the consequences are sufficiently serious, even a relatively small probability deserves attention.

Of course, uncertainty doesn’t tell us exactly which precautions to take. We need research to understand the risks better, and we need to evaluate whether our safeguards actually work. But we should also be willing to limit what a system can do while we lack that understanding—especially when giving it more autonomy or access to things through which it could cause harm.

I would put more of the burden on those developing and deploying these systems to provide evidence of safety. And that evidence should be open to independent scrutiny. It shouldn’t be enough to say, ‘We haven’t seen a catastrophe yet.’ We’re talking about systems whose capabilities are changing, so past experience may be a poor guide.

The aim is to preserve our ability to learn and to change course. We can adjust precautions as the evidence improves. But some consequences may be irreversible, and that asymmetry should matter a great deal in our decisions.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty is a reason to be cautious and that even a relatively small probability warrants attention when the potential consequences are severe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think uncertainty is actually one of the reasons to take precautions. We don’t know how to assign a reliable probability to something like losing control of very powerful AI systems. But that lack of knowledge doesn’t mean the probability is small. It means we should be careful about making decisions whose consequences could be irreversible.

We make this kind of judgment in other areas. You don’t need to know exactly how likely a major accident is before deciding that a technology needs safety testing and oversight. The amount of evidence we require should depend on the magnitude of the possible harm.

For AI, I would like us to put more of the burden on developers to demonstrate that their systems are sufficiently safe, especially as those systems become more capable and autonomous. And we need independent scientific work to evaluate those claims, rather than relying only on the companies building them.

That doesn’t mean we have to stop all AI research or give up the benefits. It means investing in safety, introducing safeguards, and being willing to slow down particular developments when we don’t understand how to control them. We can disagree about the probability of catastrophe and still agree that taking reasonable precautions is worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty is a reason to take precautions and explains that lack of a reliable probability estimate does not mean the risk is small.
